title: Senior's toolkit: hashes, HMACs and key derivation
summary: Check a download, verify a webhook signature by hand, compare MACs safely and derive keys with the right KDF.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: hashes, HMACs and key derivation
steps.body: Hashes and MACs show up at work as checksums on downloads, signatures on webhooks and keys derived from passwords. These are the commands and .NET calls people use for each.

toolkit.what: SHA-256 of files on Linux (macOS: `shasum -a 256`). Release pages publish these so you can check a download was not changed.
flags: check every file listed in a checksum file
with `-c`: skip listed files you did not download
toolkit.when: before you install a binary or trust an artifact

toolkit.what: The same on Windows PowerShell. The hash comes back in upper-case hex.
flags: the hash to use (SHA256 is the default)

toolkit.what: Hash or HMAC any input from the shell. Use it to recompute a webhook signature by hand and see who is wrong.
flags: compute HMAC with this key instead of a plain hash
raw bytes out, to pipe into `base64` when the header is Base64

toolkit.what: One-shot hashing in .NET: no object to create or dispose. There are overloads for a `Stream`, which read it to the end.
flags: hash a file or upload without loading it all
toolkit.example:
await using var file = File.OpenRead(path);
byte[] digest = await SHA256.HashDataAsync(file, ct);

toolkit.what: One-shot HMAC. The standard way to sign webhooks, cookies and API requests with a shared secret.
flags: the shared secret, at least 32 random bytes
the exact bytes that were sent, not a re-serialized copy

toolkit.what: Compare two MACs or tokens in time that does not depend on where they first differ, so an attacker cannot learn the right value byte by byte.
Feed a hash or HMAC in pieces, as data arrives, then read the result once.
flags: the final value; the object can be reused

toolkit.what: The two KDFs in the box. PBKDF2 is deliberately slow, for passwords. HKDF is fast, for turning one strong secret into several independent keys.
flags: a 32-byte key from a password (OWASP's iteration count for SHA-256)
a 32-byte key; a different `info` gives an unrelated key
toolkit.example: byte[] encKey = HKDF.DeriveKey(HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, master, 32, salt: null, info: "orders:enc:v1"u8.ToArray());

steps.prompt: SHA-256 of `abc` is the standard test vector `ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad`. What does this print?
steps.explain: SHA-256 always gives 32 bytes, whatever the input size. `ba7816bf...` is the published test vector for `abc`, worth recognising when you check an implementation.

steps.prompt: Your GitHub webhook endpoint rejects every delivery, even though the secret is right. What is the bug?
options: The MAC is computed over a re-serialized body; it must be over the exact raw bytes received
GitHub signs with SHA-1, so `HMACSHA256` can never match
steps.explain: Re-serializing changes whitespace, property order and escaping, so the bytes differ and so does the HMAC. Read the raw body first (`await new StreamReader(req.Body).ReadToEndAsync()` or into a `MemoryStream`), verify it, then parse it. To debug, recompute by hand with `openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac` on the saved raw body.

steps.prompt: Verify a webhook whose header is `sha256=<lowercase hex>`. `rawBody` holds the exact bytes received.
steps.explain: One-shot `HashData`, decode the hex the header carries, then compare bytes in constant time. `SequenceEqual` stops at the first difference, which leaks timing.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the job it is for.
pairs: check downloads against a published checksum list
recompute a webhook signature by hand
hash a 4 GB upload without loading it into memory
turn a user's password into a key
split one strong master key into per-purpose keys

steps.prompt: In review you see `HKDF.DeriveKey(HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(password), 32, salt, info)` used to make a key from a user's password. What do you say?
options: HKDF is fast, so an attacker can try billions of guesses; use a slow password KDF such as PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations or Argon2id
Fine, as long as the salt is random
Use SHA-512 instead of SHA-256 and it is safe
Fine, but the output should be 64 bytes
steps.explain: HKDF assumes its input is already high-entropy, like a random key or an ECDH secret. Passwords are low-entropy, so they need a KDF that makes each guess expensive. A salt stops precomputed tables, not fast guessing.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When a signature does not verify, save the raw bytes and recompute it with `openssl dgst` before changing code: you learn at once which side is wrong. In review, look for three things: MACs over the raw body, `FixedTimeEquals` for the comparison, and a slow KDF wherever a password goes in.
